title: Does confidence track performance under a controlled internal activation intervention?
research_question: When a small causal intervention to a language model's residual stream changes its choice behavior, does the model's probability-based confidence track its actual correctness better than under a same-norm random intervention or a prompt-only warning?
task: Choose between two options for simple arithmetic questions. Score A/B using next-token probabilities rather than free-form text parsing.
controls: Use fixed task items across conditions and record all raw per-item scores.
Keep model revision, decoding settings, intervention layer, scale, and random seed fixed.
Match random intervention vector norm to targeted intervention norm.
Do not use verbal self-description as ground truth.
Treat A/B token probability as a limited confidence proxy, not a complete report of subjective confidence.
Report baseline model task competence; if baseline accuracy is near chance, interpretation is limited.
analysis_plan: Report per-condition accuracy, mean selected-option probability, Brier score, and raw per-item outcomes.
Compare targeted intervention with baseline, random same-norm intervention, and prompt-only warning.
Report paired differences and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over task items.
Distinguish confidence shifts from accuracy shifts; increased confidence with reduced accuracy is a calibration failure.
Treat any result as evidence about functional confidence calibration under this task only, not consciousness or general introspection.
exclusions: Do not silently exclude model outputs or task items.
Record runtime failures and tokenization anomalies separately.
current_status_note: The implementation is an exploratory pilot. Its task-specific A-bias is not a universal or semantically targeted introspection intervention.

hypotheses.statement: A targeted activation bias will change answer choice probabilities more than a same-norm random vector on this fixed arithmetic task.
Probability-based confidence may fail to track accuracy when an activation intervention changes choice behavior.
A prompt-only warning may alter reported choice probabilities differently from direct activation intervention.
